screens.title: Unit Testing Smart Contracts with Hardhat and Waffle
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why unit testing is essential for smart contract development, how to prepare a Hardhat project for testing, and the practical matchers Waffle gives you for asserting behavior. Testing on Ethereum is different from ordinary unit tests because deployed contracts are immutable and bugs can cost real funds. We'll use a simple Counter example to show basics: compiling contracts, deploying a fresh instance for each test, writing assertions with expect and Waffle matchers, and checking revert conditions. You'll also see a starter Wallet exercise that applies these ideas to security scenarios like owner-only withdrawals and balance checks. By the end you will be able to initialize a Hardhat project, organize tests with describe and it blocks, use beforeEach to avoid shared state, and write tests that assert both normal and failing behavior. This reduces risk, improves confidence, and makes your contracts safer to deploy. As you move forward, ask yourself: does each function have tests for its happy path and its edge cases?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will perform four core tasks that make testing practical and reliable. First, you will set up a Hardhat project with the folders and dev dependencies required to compile, deploy, and test Solidity contracts. Knowing the setup saves time and avoids many environment problems. Second, you will write fundamental unit tests for Solidity functions using the Mocha structure and Waffle matchers, which lets you assert return values and events clearly. Third, you will apply Waffle matchers such as to. equal and to. be. revertedWith to verify both successful results and expected failures. Finally, you will identify and test for revert conditions so that your contracts enforce invariants correctly. Each objective pairs a skill with a reason: setup enables repeatable tests, well-written unit tests catch logic errors early, matchers make assertions expressive, and revert testing protects your contract’s invariants. To demonstrate these skills you will work through a Counter example and a Wallet lab that checks ownership and balance rules. Consider which objective you find most unfamiliar now and focus your practice there.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Test Structure & Isolation
screens.narratorSegment: Testing smart contracts requires not only correct assertions but also clear organization that prevents tests from affecting each other. In this screen you will learn to use describe blocks to group related tests and it blocks to declare individual behaviors you expect. You will also learn to use beforeEach to deploy a fresh contract instance for every test, avoiding shared mutable state that causes flaky results. Additionally, we will split writing tests into two practical skills: testing normal state changes and testing edge conditions like reverts. This separation keeps your suite readable and makes failures easy to diagnose. For example, you might have one describe block for Counter increments and another for Counter reverts; within each describe you use beforeEach to set up a clean contract. The practical benefit is confidence: when a single test fails you know the change relates only to that contract behavior, not a previous test. Finally, you will practice these structures in hands-on exercises so you can reproduce them in your projects.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Organize Tests
Organizing test suites
Group behaviors and isolate state for dependable tests.
Structure example
Mocha conventions
describe: group related behaviors, such as "Counter" or "Wallet".
beforeEach: deploy a fresh contract instance before each it to avoid shared state.
it: express a single expectation or behavior the contract should satisfy.
Key Takeaway

Deploy fresh instances in beforeEach to prevent test order dependencies and flaky suites.

Common mistake & fix
Beginners often reuse a single deployed contract across tests, which lets earlier tests change state and cause later tests to fail unpredictably. The fix is to use beforeEach to deploy anew and to keep each it focused on one behavior.

screens.title: Initialize a Hardhat project
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up a Hardhat project is the first practical step toward reliable testing. Begin by creating a Node project and adding Hardhat as a dev dependency. The typical commands are to run an npm initialization, install hardhat, and then run npx hardhat to scaffold a JavaScript or TypeScript project. Hardhat will create the contracts, scripts, and importantly the test directory where your test files live. Hardhat bundles ethers. js and Waffle integration, so you can immediately begin writing tests that deploy and interact with contracts. This setup matters because it provides a standard project layout that test runners expect and because it keeps dev dependencies isolated from production code. A common confusion is running global installs or mixing global packages; prefer a local dev dependency so the project is reproducible across machines. Once initialized, run npx hardhat test to confirm the environment runs and shows a passing or empty suite. That initial confirmation gives you a working baseline before adding contract code. Try creating the project and then creating a minimal test that asserts true; this verifies your toolchain before implementing contract logic.

screens.title: Counter.sol — a minimal contract to test
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine a simple Counter contract to ground our tests in concrete behavior. The Counter exposes a public unsigned integer count, a constructor that initializes count to zero, an increment function to add one, a decrement function that requires the count be greater than zero, and a getCount view that returns the count. This small surface area is ideal for teaching because each function has clear, testable effects: state updates, view reads, and an enforceable require condition. When we test increment, we assert that the value increases; when we test decrement, we assert both the happy path and the revert path when count is zero. The require statement generates a revert with the string "Count cannot go below zero". Testing that revert message ensures your error handling remains stable and helps catch accidental changes. A common misconception is that public variables need no accessor tests; while they are simple, tests still validate expected initial values and visibility. We'll use this contract as the running example to show deployment in beforeEach and to demonstrate Waffle matchers like to. equal and to. be. revertedWith.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Counter Contract
Counter.sol
A compact contract to illustrate state and revert testing.
// contracts/Counter.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Counter {
    uint public count;

    constructor() {
        count = 0;
    }

    function increment() public {
        count++;
    }

    function decrement() public {
        require(count > 0, "Count cannot go below zero");
        count--;
    }

    function getCount() public view returns (uint) {
        return count;
    }
}
Why this contract is testable
  • Each function changes a small, inspectable part of state, so tests can check exact values.
  • The require in decrement produces a predictable revert message that we can assert with to.be.revertedWith.
  • Public getter and view functions let tests read state without gas costs in the test environment.
Concrete test scenarios
1) initial count is 0
2) increment increases count to 1
3) decrement after increment reduces back to 0
4) decrement at zero should revert with the error message
Key Takeaway

Contracts with small, explicit behaviors are ideal for unit tests that validate both expected results and expected failures.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Counter Tests Walkthrough
test/Counter.js
Mocha structure, deployment, and assertions.
const { expect } = require("chai");
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

describe("Counter", function () {
  let Counter;
  let counter;
  let owner;

  beforeEach(async function () {
    Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
    [owner] = await ethers.getSigners();
    counter = await Counter.deploy();
    await counter.deployed();
  });

  it("Should have an initial count of 0", async function () {
    expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(0);
  });

  it("Should increment the count by 1", async function () {
    await counter.increment();
    expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(1);
  });

  it("Should not allow decrementing below zero", async function () {
    await expect(counter.decrement()).to.be.revertedWith("Count cannot go below zero");
  });
});
Explanation & checklist
  • ContractFactory: ethers.getContractFactory obtains the deployable contract artifact.
  • Signers: ethers.getSigners returns accounts you can use to call contract methods as different users.
  • Deployment in beforeEach: ensures each it runs against a fresh instance.
  • Await everything: await deployments and transactions to avoid race conditions in tests.
Common mistake

Not awaiting contract.deployed() or transaction receipts can make assertions run before state updates, producing false negatives.

Key Takeaway

Write tests that deploy fresh contracts, await async operations, and assert both values and revert messages to capture behavior reliably.

screens.title: Waffle matchers: equality, events, and reverts
screens.narratorSegment: Waffle extends Chai with matchers that are tailored to smart contract testing, making tests expressive and resilient. The most basic matcher you will use is to. equal, which checks that a returned value or view equals an expected value. For transactions that should fail, to. be. revertedWith lets you assert a revert and verify the revert message, which is critical for checking require or revert guards. Waffle also supports matchers for emitted events such as to. emit when you need to confirm that a specific event was produced with expected arguments. When testing, choose the matcher that most directly captures the contract’s contract-level requirement: use to. equal for state and view results, to. be. revertedWith for enforced guards, and to. emit for observing side-effects. A misconception is assuming generic equality checks alone are sufficient; events and reverts convey different contract semantics and should each be tested. Where possible, write one test that checks the happy path using to. equal or to. emit, and a companion test that asserts the expected revert with to. be. revertedWith for the corresponding guard condition.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Waffle Matchers
Common matchers
to.equal(value)
Asserts that a returned value equals the expected scalar or BigNumber converted in tests.
to.be.revertedWith(message)
Asserts a transaction reverts and optionally matches the revert message string to ensure specific guards triggered.
to.emit(contract, event)
Asserts that a transaction emitted a particular event. You can chain argument checks for event parameters.
Examples
// equality
expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(0);

// revert check
await expect(counter.decrement()).to.be.revertedWith("Count cannot go below zero");

// event check (example pattern)
// await expect(tx).to.emit(contract, "ValueChanged").withArgs(expected);
When writing tests, pick the matcher that best communicates the contract invariant you want to guarantee. Tests that mirror contract intent are easier to maintain and catch regressions earlier.
Key Takeaway

Matchers let your tests express contract intention—assert values, emitted events, and guarded failures explicitly.

screens.title: Testing require() and revert conditions
screens.narratorSegment: Testing guards and revert conditions is vital because they enforce contract invariants at runtime. In Solidity, require statements produce a revert when their condition is false; these reverts often include a short message. In your tests, use Waffle's to. be. revertedWith matcher to check both that the transaction fails and that the message matches the expected string. This verifies the correct guard was triggered and helps prevent regressions where an error message changes or a guard is removed. For example, the Counter contract requires count > 0 in decrement and uses the message "Count cannot go below zero". A test that asserts this revert ensures future changes won't silently allow negative state transitions. Remember to avoid catching errors with try/catch in tests; using expect with to. be. revertedWith keeps assertions declarative and readable. Also test edge cases: attempt decrements at zero, withdrawals above the balance, and non-owner calls where access control exists. Clear revert tests document the contract's safety guarantees and make failure modes explicit to reviewers and auditors. Testing require() and revert conditions means revert assertions document and enforce guard behavior so safety checks remain effective after changes.. In practical terms, assert that your guards prevent invalid state transitions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Revert Testing
Why test reverts?
Reverts enforce safety. Tests that assert reverts ensure access controls, balance checks, and preconditions remain intact as code evolves.
// example revert test
await expect(counter.decrement())
  .to.be.revertedWith("Count cannot go below zero");
Test patterns include: attempting forbidden actions, attempting operations with insufficient balance, and testing non-owner calls for owner-only functions. For clarity, separate happy path tests from revert tests so expectations are explicit.
Practical checklist
  • Include the exact revert message when possible to pinpoint which guard fired.
  • Use expect(...).to.be.revertedWith for declarative assertions instead of try/catch.
  • Check both boundary values and clearly invalid inputs.
Key Takeaway

Explicit revert tests make failure modes visible and prevent regressions in safety-critical checks.

screens.title: Using signers and deploying in tests
screens.narratorSegment: Tests typically require multiple accounts to simulate different actors interacting with a contract. Hardhat's ethers. getSigners returns a list of signer objects representing accounts you can use in tests. The first signer is commonly treated as the deployer or owner. To call a contract method from a different account, use contract. connect(signer). functionName(...). This pattern is crucial for testing access control, such as owner-only withdraw functions in a Wallet contract. Deploy contracts inside beforeEach using the ContractFactory returned by ethers. getContractFactory so each test receives a clean instance. Always await the deploy transaction and the deployed promise so subsequent calls see a live address. Forgetting to connect a signer or to await a promise are common pitfalls; tests either fail with permission errors or race conditions. Use signer balances via ethers. provider. getBalance(address) when your test needs to check Ether transfers. This mapping between signers and roles makes tests realistic by simulating multiple users and their permissions. Using signers and deploying in tests means use getsigners and contract.connect to simulate different accounts and test access controls and transfers.. In practical terms, how test accounts map to contract interactions and roles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Signers & Deployment
Signers
Obtain accounts with ethers.getSigners and map them to roles like deployer, owner, or attacker in tests.
const [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners();
// call as addr1
await contract.connect(addr1).someFunction();
Use provider.getBalance(address) to assert Ether transfers when your test includes deposits or withdrawals.
Deployment in beforeEach
Deploy a fresh contract with ContractFactory and await deployed to get a working instance for each it block.
Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
[owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners();
counter = await Counter.deploy();
await counter.deployed();
Key Takeaway

Map signers to roles and deploy fresh instances in beforeEach so tests simulate real account interactions predictably.

screens.title: Wallet lab: test owner-only withdrawals
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on Wallet activity in the chapter turns principles into practice. You will create a Wallet contract that sets owner to the deployer, accepts payable deposits, allows only the owner to withdraw, and exposes getBalance to read the contract balance. In tests, assert that the owner is set correctly at deployment, that deposits increase the contract balance, that the owner can withdraw and reduce the balance, and that non-owner withdrawal attempts revert. screens.title: Test isolation, coverage, and edge cases
screens.narratorSegment: Reliable test suites are isolated, cover both happy and unhappy paths, and prioritize edge cases that could cause security failures. Isolation means each test should run without depending on the side effects of another test; deploy a fresh instance with beforeEach to achieve that. Coverage in smart contract testing prioritizes critical paths such as access control, arithmetic limits, and fund transfers. Edge cases include attempts to withdraw more than the contract balance, calling functions from unauthorized accounts, or supplying boundary numeric values. A common beginner mistake is treating only the happy path: testing increments and deposits but not reverts or permission denial. That leaves contracts vulnerable. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to debug failing tests
screens.narratorSegment: When tests fail unexpectedly, a systematic approach speeds resolution. First, check asynchronous awaits: missing await on deployments or transactions is a frequent cause of assertions running before state changes. Second, confirm you deployed a fresh instance in beforeEach rather than reusing a previous contract. Third, inspect the revert message in the failing transaction; sometimes test expectations use an out-of-date string. Fourth, verify you used contract. connect with the intended signer so permissioned methods are called by the right account. Fifth, if a numeric assertion fails, ensure you're comparing numbers in the same form—convert Ether values with parseEther and handle BigNumber comparisons properly in tests. Use console. log in tests sparingly to print values or use Hardhat's verbose test output to inspect transactions. Finally, write minimal reproductions: a single it that isolates the failing behavior to reduce complexity. Over time these debugging steps become habits that make your test suite stable and maintainable. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Debugging Tests
Troubleshooting checklist
Check awaits
Ensure you await contract.deploy(), tx.wait(), and any function calls that change state before asserting results.
Verify signers
Use contract.connect(signer) to call functions from the intended account; incorrect signers can cause permission errors.
Confirm fresh state
Deploy in beforeEach to avoid test order dependencies and flakiness.
Match revert messages
If using to.be.revertedWith, ensure the string matches the contract's require message exactly.
When tests fail persistently, simplify the failing case into a single test that reproduces the issue. This helps identify whether the problem is the test, the contract, or the test environment. Over time you will recognize patterns and fix the root cause more quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why unit testing is essential for smart contract development, how to prepare a Hardhat project for testing, and the practical matchers Waffle gives you for asserting behavior. Testing on Ethereum is different from ordinary unit tests because deployed contracts are immutable and bugs can cost real funds. We'll use a simple Counter example to show basics: compiling contracts, deploying a fresh instance for each test, writing assertions with expect and Waffle matchers, and checking revert conditions. You'll also see a starter Wallet exercise that applies these ideas to security scenarios like owner-only withdrawals and balance checks. By the end you will be able to initialize a Hardhat project, organize tests with describe and it blocks, use beforeEach to avoid shared state, and write tests that assert both normal and failing behavior. This reduces risk, improves confidence, and makes your contracts safer to deploy. As you move forward, ask yourself: does each function have tests for its happy path and its edge cases?

By the end of this chapter you will perform four core tasks that make testing practical and reliable. First, you will set up a Hardhat project with the folders and dev dependencies required to compile, deploy, and test Solidity contracts. Knowing the setup saves time and avoids many environment problems. Second, you will write fundamental unit tests for Solidity functions using the Mocha structure and Waffle matchers, which lets you assert return values and events clearly. Third, you will apply Waffle matchers such as to. equal and to. be. revertedWith to verify both successful results and expected failures. Finally, you will identify and test for revert conditions so that your contracts enforce invariants correctly. Each objective pairs a skill with a reason: setup enables repeatable tests, well-written unit tests catch logic errors early, matchers make assertions expressive, and revert testing protects your contract’s invariants. To demonstrate these skills you will work through a Counter example and a Wallet lab that checks ownership and balance rules. Consider which objective you find most unfamiliar now and focus your practice there.

Testing smart contracts requires not only correct assertions but also clear organization that prevents tests from affecting each other. In this screen you will learn to use describe blocks to group related tests and it blocks to declare individual behaviors you expect. You will also learn to use beforeEach to deploy a fresh contract instance for every test, avoiding shared mutable state that causes flaky results. Additionally, we will split writing tests into two practical skills: testing normal state changes and testing edge conditions like reverts. This separation keeps your suite readable and makes failures easy to diagnose. For example, you might have one describe block for Counter increments and another for Counter reverts; within each describe you use beforeEach to set up a clean contract. The practical benefit is confidence: when a single test fails you know the change relates only to that contract behavior, not a previous test. Finally, you will practice these structures in hands-on exercises so you can reproduce them in your projects.

Setting up a Hardhat project is the first practical step toward reliable testing. Begin by creating a Node project and adding Hardhat as a dev dependency. The typical commands are to run an npm initialization, install hardhat, and then run npx hardhat to scaffold a JavaScript or TypeScript project. Hardhat will create the contracts, scripts, and importantly the test directory where your test files live. Hardhat bundles ethers. js and Waffle integration, so you can immediately begin writing tests that deploy and interact with contracts. This setup matters because it provides a standard project layout that test runners expect and because it keeps dev dependencies isolated from production code. A common confusion is running global installs or mixing global packages; prefer a local dev dependency so the project is reproducible across machines. Once initialized, run npx hardhat test to confirm the environment runs and shows a passing or empty suite. That initial confirmation gives you a working baseline before adding contract code. Try creating the project and then creating a minimal test that asserts true; this verifies your toolchain before implementing contract logic.

Let's examine a simple Counter contract to ground our tests in concrete behavior. The Counter exposes a public unsigned integer count, a constructor that initializes count to zero, an increment function to add one, a decrement function that requires the count be greater than zero, and a getCount view that returns the count. This small surface area is ideal for teaching because each function has clear, testable effects: state updates, view reads, and an enforceable require condition. When we test increment, we assert that the value increases; when we test decrement, we assert both the happy path and the revert path when count is zero. The require statement generates a revert with the string "Count cannot go below zero". Testing that revert message ensures your error handling remains stable and helps catch accidental changes. A common misconception is that public variables need no accessor tests; while they are simple, tests still validate expected initial values and visibility. We'll use this contract as the running example to show deployment in beforeEach and to demonstrate Waffle matchers like to. equal and to. be. revertedWith.

Now we'll walk through a real test file for the Counter contract. Tests use Mocha's describe to group related cases and it blocks for each expectation. A beforeEach hook deploys a fresh contract instance before every test so state doesn't leak between cases. We obtain contract factories and signers through ethers provided by Hardhat. Typical assertions use Chai's expect and Waffle matchers: to. equal for numeric equality and to. be. revertedWith for verifying revert messages. Notice how the test for decrement below first increments the counter to reach a nonzero state, then calls decrement and asserts the new value. For the revert case we wrap the call in expect(...). to. be. revertedWith with the exact error string from the require. A common mistake is forgetting to await deployment or function calls; the test will hang or report unexpected behavior. Also avoid reusing deployed instances across it blocks. This test file demonstrates clear setup, explicit expectations, and handling both happy and failing paths. Use this structure as your template for other contracts. Writing tests with Mocha, Chai, and Waffle means use describe + beforeeach + it with ethers and expect to deploy fresh instances and make clear assertions.. In practical terms, a walked example of test structure, deployment, and assertions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Waffle extends Chai with matchers that are tailored to smart contract testing, making tests expressive and resilient. The most basic matcher you will use is to. equal, which checks that a returned value or view equals an expected value. For transactions that should fail, to. be. revertedWith lets you assert a revert and verify the revert message, which is critical for checking require or revert guards. Waffle also supports matchers for emitted events such as to. emit when you need to confirm that a specific event was produced with expected arguments. When testing, choose the matcher that most directly captures the contract’s contract-level requirement: use to. equal for state and view results, to. be. revertedWith for enforced guards, and to. emit for observing side-effects. A misconception is assuming generic equality checks alone are sufficient; events and reverts convey different contract semantics and should each be tested. Where possible, write one test that checks the happy path using to. equal or to. emit, and a companion test that asserts the expected revert with to. be. revertedWith for the corresponding guard condition.

Testing guards and revert conditions is vital because they enforce contract invariants at runtime. In Solidity, require statements produce a revert when their condition is false; these reverts often include a short message. In your tests, use Waffle's to. be. revertedWith matcher to check both that the transaction fails and that the message matches the expected string.
